segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: They're still laying flat. Nobody moved.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So what happens next?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She's talking, right? This isn't how it was supposed to be. And she's also crying. And she's talking to herself. I remember it being very hard to follow what she was saying.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And eventually, I said, I'm sorry, I think you have the wrong room. And she started to cry. And she said, I know, I know. I do this, I do this. I don't know why I do this.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And then she's pacing back and forth, and kind of crying. And she sits down on the bed, at the foot of the bed.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Did she seem crazy, or did she seem upset?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I mean, it's interesting. I was-- I think I-- I was too young and unfamiliar to identify what a crazy person seems like.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: But what I could identify in that moment was that this person was unpredictable.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So you guys were like, oh, I've got to be really careful how I do this.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I remember feeling that pressure, and in that moment, very, very, very aware of my brothers and sisters, because they were so little. And--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: --that something bad could happen to them. And that the way that it wasn't going to happen to them was me. There were no adults there. I think it was the first situation I was ever in where there was-- you couldn't defer to someone else to keep you safe or tell you what to do. And what do I do?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And it had that quality of like-- like, time slows down. And you're kind of-- you're there, but you're also watching. And so then, I did the math in my head. And I was like, OK, I have a couple options. They are cry for help, scream. But I don't think anyone will hear.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Mhm.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I remember looking at how far away the phone was from me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Mhm.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And I realized I can reach and grab the phone, and I could call for help. Or even like, if I could knock on the door where my sister was--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Sister in the connecting room next door.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I could at least-- they would know something was happening in here. And they could get to us in time.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: But all of that felt like an escalation, like I would provoke her. And so what can I do to not provoke her and kind of play up the fact that we're children? And what I felt I needed to do was I needed to calm her down and become her friend. And if I could become her friend, she would leave, and she wouldn't hurt us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Like, get her to see you as a person?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Just make her think I was on her side. Because then-- it didn't feel like she didn't see us as people. It just felt like-- it felt dangerous, and I didn't understand why. And I felt like the key to being safe was slowing everything down.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And I remember her saying, I'm really sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry I'm here. I'm sorry I'm doing this. I'm sorry.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Mhm.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And I don't remember this, but my brother remembers that what she said was, I'm sorry, girls. I'm sorry, girls. And that his whole memory of this night was just being like, I'm a boy. [LAUGHS] He was so mad.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And so I ask her-- I said, are you OK? Is everything OK? And that's-- she kept, you know, going on about how her night was so hard.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And I was like, I'm so sorry. That sounds really, really difficult.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And this is you trying to befriend her.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yeah, this is me trying to befriend her. But it's weird, I feel like-- I was hyper alert to like, if I can understand what's going on with her, I can help solve it. But I couldn't understand, because it didn't make any sense.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Did you feel sorry for her?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I felt concerned for her.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And-- and then she took out her purse. And she reached into her purse, and then she gripped onto something. And I remember thinking like, oh no, like, what-- the way-- like, if that--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, like, it's like a gun or something.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Right, gun, or a knife or something. I remember my heart just dropping. And then she pulled out a hairbrush. And then she just started brushing her hair, like, at the foot of my bed.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And-- and then at that point, I was like, this is really weird. Like, this is like--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And I don't think she's going to leave. And then she sat on the vanity in front of the mirror, at the desk. And she took her earrings off. And--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, wow.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And she started like-- she took her shoes off. She took her coat off. She was just like--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, wow.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: --making herself comfortable to like, be here now.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And so I let her do all that, and was sort of listening to her go on about what was wrong. And then eventually, after I felt like enough time had passed, I said, we have to wake up early to go to school tomorrow. And we're really tired, so I think we should probably go back to bed now.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And she was like, I know, I know. I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I'm sorry I'm here. I'm here. I'm sorry I'm here. And I said, no, it's totally fine that you're here-- almost like, you know, thank you for being here. But do you mind leaving now?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And so I very slowly stood up and walked over to the door. And every moment was like making sure I was safe. And then I open the door.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And she said, OK, OK. And she put her shoes on, and then she started to leave. And just as she was about to leave, I said, oh, you forgot your earrings. And then she was like-- started crying all over again, like it was this huge thing, walked over to get the earrings, and then sat back down on the bed.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And I remember thinking like, goddamn, why did I bring up the earrings? We were so close to being safe. So then the whole thing-- basically, the whole thing started all over again, where I had to like, listen to her cry, calm her down. And then finally, I'm like, you know, we have to wake up early to go to school. Do you mind leaving?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And I walked her to the door. And she walked out of the door. And then as soon as she was out of the door, I just pushed the door as hard as I could to close it. And when I pushed it, like basically slammed it shut, she screamed at the top of her lungs.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And is there a bolt or something on the door?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I think I did bolt it after I slammed it shut.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And then I heard her screaming in the hallway. And then she ran down the hallway, screaming. And then she ran back towards the door, screaming. And--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That must have been terrifying.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: It was so scary. And then-- then it got-- was quiet. And then I heard this loud-- she's like banging on the door, like as hard as she can, right?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And then I hear a voice, and it's my dad. And my dad's like, open the door. Open the door. And I realize it's not her banging on the door.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: So I open the door. And my dad's standing there, and he's like, did you hear someone screaming in the hallway? So then I tell him this whole story.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I'm like, there was this woman. She was in our room. I tell him all the details. And he is furious. He was so mad.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And then he told us to stay there, shut the door, don't open the door. And then he went downstairs and talked to the hotel about it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah, what did he learn?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: They tell him that she had been outside. She was crying. They asked if she was a guest there. She said yes, her name was Elena Baker. And so they looked up the name.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Elena Baker?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Elena Baker, yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And your name is Elna Baker.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: But I don't believe this part of the story. I think someone at the hotel just said this to him to cover.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then they gave her a key?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And then they gave her a key.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yeah. And so the hotel offered him, you know, the whole stay for free, everything for free. And he's like, I don't care about your money. I want you guys to do a formal investigation as to how this happened.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wow, that's such a white-man-takes-charge move.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: My dad's not white.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, point taken. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: He's a Hispanic man.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I was just thinking, you just never hear like, somebody be like, I demand a formal investigation, you know what I mean? It's like he's a member of Congress or something, you know?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: All right, anyway--

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: But that's what-- I mean, that's totally how my dad would-- like, that's my dad.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Point taken. OK.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And so they do a formal investigation, which they then send to my dad. And--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Long after you've like, gone from the hotel.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Exactly. And in it, there's a picture of the woman. And then there's her history.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She had been in a psychiatric hospital and escaped that night, come to the hotel. And she had a long history of breaking into people's homes. And he's not certain about this part, so I don't--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He doesn't remember it?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: He doesn't remember, but he says that he remembers there being-- she had attacked people when she'd broken into their homes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's what he remembers?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: That's what he remembers.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That part of the story-- the investigation, who the woman was-- Elna only found that out a couple of years ago when she asked her dad about it. At the time, back when she was 14, her parents kept all that from her and her brother and sisters. They didn't want them to dwell on it or make them afraid of the world. They didn't want that evening to become a bigger deal than it already was. And Elna says today, that worked.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And it's funny, I've-- even as I've told this story over the years, people are like, oh, that's so traumatic, or that's crazy. And I don't think of it like that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: How so?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: It just-- it just was sort of like a-- because nothing bad happened, it has no category for me, if that makes sense. It's been easier-- it was easier to just think like, oh, this one-- this weird thing happened one night when we were in a hotel.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In retrospect, would you have preferred if they had told you back when you were 14?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: No, I think it's good that I got to live in a world that I think is safe.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: On the other hand, she says, if they had made clear how much danger she was in, the family's memory of it and her memory of it wouldn't be of this weird event with no category, this random thing that happened one night. Instead, it would fit squarely into the category called victory-- solid win for 14-year-old girl in a big, religious family, when she got that stranger out of their hotel room without anybody getting hurt. And Elna says she would have liked that win.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When you're trapped inside a room with an unpredictable person, really, all you've got is your wits, and your ability to read the situation, and your judgment at guessing what will work. Nice to show everybody that even a kid can make the right call sometimes, if they pay attention closely enough.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Elna Baker, one of the producers of our show, talking to Ira Glass.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Act three-- You Can't Go Your Own Way. In her memoir, In the Dream House, Carmen Maria Machado wrote this chapter that's set up like a choose your own adventure story, which I just thought was so smart when I read it. In it, she imagines different choices she could have made with a partner that she's in a bad relationship with-- an abusive relationship.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And one of the things it captures is just the mental energy that somebody in that situation can end up putting into trying to figure out what they should do or not do to avoid setting off their partner. A heads up that this excerpt includes a scene with sexual content. It's read for us by actor Zoe Winters.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: Page one. You wake up, and the air is milky and bright. The room glows with a kind of effervescent contentment, despite the boxes, and clothes, and dishes. You think to yourself, this is the kind of morning you could get used to.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: When you turn over, she is staring at you. The luminous innocence of the light curdles in your stomach. You don't remember ever going from awake to afraid so quickly.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: You were moving all night, she says. Your arms and elbows touched me. You kept me awake.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: If you apologize profusely, go to page two. If you tell her to wake you up next time your elbows touch her in your sleep, go to page three. If you tell her to calm down, go to page five.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: I choose page two. Page two-- I'm so sorry, you tell her. I really didn't mean to. I just move my arms around a lot in my sleep.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: You try to be light about it. Did you know my dad does the same thing? The sleeping damsel swoon. So weird. I must have--

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: Are you really sorry? She says. I don't think you are. I am, you say.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: You want the first impression of the morning to return to you-- its freshness, its light. I really am. Prove it. How? Stop doing it.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: I told you, I can't. Fuck you, she says, and gets out of bed. You follow her all the way to the kitchen. Go to page seven.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: Page seven-- breakfast. You scramble some eggs, make some toast. She eats mechanically and leaves the plate on the table. Clean that up, she says, as she goes to the bedroom to get dressed.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: If you stare mutely at the dirty plate, and all you can think about is Clara Barton, the feminist icon of your youth, who had to teach herself how to be a nurse, and endured abuse from men telling her what to do at every turn, and you remember being so angry, and running to your parents and asking them if women still got told what was right or proper, and your mom said yes, and your dad said no, and you, for the first time, had an inkling of how complicated and terrible the world was, go to page 10. If you do as you are told, go to page eight. If you tell her to do it herself, go to page five.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: Page five-- are you kidding? You'd never do this. Don't try to convince any of these people that you'd stand up for yourself for one second. Get out of here. Go to the next chapter. You're out.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: Wait, no, let's try that again. I go to page eight. Page eight-- as you're washing the dishes, you think to yourself, maybe I should put a tack on my forehead. Maybe I should be a better person. Go to page one.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: I go to page three. Page three-- baby, if this ever happens in the future, you can always wake me up, and I'll go to the couch, I promise. I really don't mean to do it. I don't have any memory of it. I can't control how I move in my sleep.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: You are such a fucking cunt, she says. You never take responsibility for anything. All you have to do is wake me up, you say, a kind of incoherent desperation zipping through your skull. That's it. Wake me up and tell me to move or sleep on the couch, and I will do it. I swear to you.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: If you do as you are told, go to page eight. If you tell her to do it herself, go to page five. If you stare mutely at the dirty plate, and all you can think about is Clara Barton, the feminist icon of your youth, who had to teach herself how to be a nurse, and endured abuse from men telling her what to do at every turn, and you remember being so angry, and running to your parents and asking them if women still got told what was right or proper, and your mom said yes, and your dad said no, and you, for the first time, had an inkling of how complicated and terrible the world was, go to page 10.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: Page 10-- that night, she [MUTED] you as you lie there mutely, praying for it to be over, praying she won't notice you're gone. You have voided your body so many times by now that it is force of habit, reflexive as a sigh. It reminds you of your first boyfriend, who [MUTED] you while watching porn, how he rutted and rutted, and then every so often, lifted the remote to rewind something you couldn't see.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: Once, you turned your head over the lip of the bed and saw a tangle of upside-down limbs, and your brain couldn't make sense of them. You never looked again. You would just lie there silently, watching his face move over you. It was like being unfolded beneath the yawn of the planetarium as a kid-- the sped-up rotation of the Earth, the movement of the stars, the constellations melting into and out of being.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: You shudder and moan with precision. She turns off the lights. You watch the darkness until the darkness leaves you, or you leave it.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: To sleep, go to page 14. To dream about the present, go to page 13. To dream about the future, go to page 12.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: To dream about the past, go to page 11. I want to dream about the past. I choose page 11.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: Page 11-- the first time it happened. The first time she yelled at you so much you were crying within 30 seconds from waking-- a record. She said, the first 10 minutes of the day, I'm not responsible for anything I say. This struck you as poetic. You even wrote it down, sure you would find a place for it in a book, maybe. Go to page 14.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: Page 9-- you shouldn't be on this page. There's no way to get here from the choices given to you. Do you think that, by flipping through this chapter linearly, you'd find some kind of relief? Don't you get it? All of this shit already happened. And you can't make it not happen, no matter what you do.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: Do you want a picture of a fawn? Will that help? OK, here's a fawn. She is small, and dappled, and loose-legged.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: She hears a sound, freezes, and then bolts. She knows what to do. She knows there's somewhere safer she can be. Go to page 10.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: I don't want to go to page 10. Page 6-- you shouldn't be on this page. There's no way to get here from the choices given to you. You flipped here because you got sick of the cycle.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: You wanted to get out. You're smarter than me. Go to page 10.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: Fine. I go to page 10. Page 10-- that night, she fucks you as you lie there mutely, praying for it to be over, praying she won't notice you're gone. You have voided your body so many times by now that it is force of habit, reflexive as a sigh.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: It reminds you of your first-- the sped-up rotation of the Earth, the movement of the stars, the constellations melting into and out of being. You shudder and moan with precision. She turns off the lights. You watch the darkness until the darkness leaves you, or you leave it.

segments.text: To sleep, go to page 14. To dream about the past, go to page 11. To dream about the present, go to page 13.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: Page 13-- you shouldn't be here, but it's OK. It's a dream. She can't find you here. In a minute, you're going to wake up, and everything is going to seem like it's the same, but it's not.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: There's a way out. Are you listening to me? You can't forget when you wake up. You can't go to page 14.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: I want to dream about the future. I go to page 12. Page 12-- it's going to be all right.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: One day, your wife will gently adjust your arm if it touches her face at night, soothingly straightening it while kissing you. Sometimes, you will wake up just enough to notice. Other times, she'll only tell you in the morning. It's the kind of morning you could get used to. Go to page 14.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: Page 14-- you wake up, and the air is milky and bright. The room glows with a kind of effervescent contentment, despite the boxes, and clothes, and dishes. You think to yourself, this is the kind of morning you could get used to.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: You were moving all night, she says. Your arms and elbows touched me. You kept me awake.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: If you apologize profusely, go to page two. If you tell her to wake you up next time your elbows touch her in your sleep, go to page three. If you toss back the blankets from your body and hit the floor with both feet, and tear through the house like it's Pamplona, and when you get to the driveway, your car keys are already in your hand, and you drive away with a theatrical squeal of the tires, never to return again, go to page 15.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: Page 15-- that's not how it happened, but OK, we can pretend. I'll give it to you, just this once. Turn to page 16.

segments.speaker: Zoe Winters
segments.text: Page 16-- an end. In the pit of it, you fantasize about dying-- tripping on a sidewalk, and stumbling into the path of an oncoming car, a gas leak silently offing you in your sleep, a machete-wielding madman on public transit, falling down the stairs, but drunk, so you flop, limb over limb, like a marionette, and feel no pain-- anything to make it stop. You have forgotten that leaving is an option.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Zoe Winters reading a chapter from Carmen Maria Machado's memoir, In the Dream House. Carmen has a comic series out now called The Low, Low Woods, from DC Comics. You can see Zoe Winters in season three of HBO'S Succession, which is out in October.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Act four-- Blue Kid on the Block. This last story is about what happens after you get out-- in this particular case, when you get out of Rochester, New York. The kid in this story, who we're going to call Leo-- it's not his real name-- his family had moved to an entirely different state. And he was not happy about it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: At the time, Leo was just starting seventh grade. He was having a harder time finding his place in middle school than other middle school kids, because, you know, he was new to town, but also because Leo still loved Rochester. He loved his school there. He loved his friends. Suddenly, everything about his life was different, and according to Leo, much worse.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The signature on his Gmail account now read, Rochester is much better, in big, red letters. Sarah Koenig knows Leo and his parents. She visited them at home to see how Leo is doing.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: This is how much Leo does not want to be here-- when I got to his house, he was on the sofa with a laptop, investigating Greyhound bus schedules. His mother was going to drive him and his sister back to Rochester for the Columbus Day weekend, but not until Saturday morning. And Leo wanted to get there Friday for more time with his friends.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: A multi-stage negotiation followed with his dad. For one thing, a bus ticket costs money.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: That's not the-- that's not a problem. [? I have that money-- ?]

segments.speaker: Leo's Dad
segments.text: Not for you. No, that wasn't a problem for you.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: No, but--

segments.speaker: Leo's Dad
segments.text: There isn't one, right?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: There isn't one-- not at 6:15 in the morning. And you won't let me miss school on Friday.

segments.speaker: Leo's Dad
segments.text: The bus takes eight hours. Even if you left at noon, you'd be at-- are gonna do the math? That's excellent.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Never mind that the bus takes twice as long as driving, and never mind that Leo would be alone, and have to change buses, and that his parents had no intention of letting him go through with this plan. But it's the kind of negotiation you indulge when your kid is miserable. And Leo is miserable. He told me right away he was, and that he had been from the moment he got here in August.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Is this the first time you've-- in your life where you felt like you've been sad about something for this long?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: I think so, except for maybe when my other cat died-- my old cat.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: And does this feel worse than that?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Mhm. I've never had long periods of sad until now. I don't know. I don't know anyone here, really. And I think it's just everything in general that's overwhelming.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Back in Rochester, Leo had known all his best friends since kindergarten or before. They played together at school, after school, on weekends. Everybody knew everybody. Everything was comfortable.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: And as a sixth grader in his old school, he and his friends were at the top of the heap. They wore green sashes in the morning, and got to be door monitors for the younger kids coming into the building. So imagine now, Leo takes a school bus for the first time to his new school, a sprawling one-story building full of sixth, seventh, and eighth graders.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Leo's small for his age, only a hair taller than his sister, who's only nine years old. On day one, he knows exactly no one.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: It was much louder than my old school, much louder. People talking, people closing and opening lockers. People walking-- it was just noise. Just older kids, more kids, because my old school was tiny.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Leo is between. He's old enough to decipher Greyhound bus schedules, but not old enough to actually travel on one by himself, and old enough to know that, if he's going to survive in middle school, he has to make friends, but that making those friends stands to be significantly more complicated than it was back in Rochester. Leo's sister, Auden, is in fourth grade. He says she's not having as hard a time of it.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: She hasn't been alive as long. She hasn't made as deep connections. And she's already met some-- a friend in her school. I think it's easier to make friends in elementary school than in middle school.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Oh, really? Why?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Because people care less about who you are.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: What do you mean by that?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: The older you get, the more you judge people on their looks, their background, their-- how they act, like, what cool is for kids. Because in kindergarten, you could just walk up to someone and say, do you want to be my friend? And they would-- then, that would be it. But it's harder.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: I just think people are more wary before they open up. They like-- I don't know, in first grade, if I met someone, I wouldn't really care who they were. I would just care if they were nice or not.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: The day I interviewed him, Leo had had a couple of breakthroughs. He emailed his parents during the school day to tell them the first piece of good news they'd had from him. Until that day, the emails had mostly been three desperate words-- I feel awful. Without even a period at the end to make the feeling finite, it was an endless awful.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: But on this Thursday, he wrote to tell them the mashed potatoes they serve in the cafeteria were great, followed by four exclamation points. Second-- and this was the big news-- he asked another kid if he wanted to come over. Leo told me he thought about it first for a few days, then finally emailed the boy, whose name is Devin, another seventh grader.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: But now, Leo didn't want to call Devin's house to finalize a plan. He dreaded the awkwardness of the phone. So his dad called Devin's parents, introduced himself as Leo's father.

segments.speaker: Leo's Dad
segments.text: --dad. He goes to school with your son, Evan. And we were-- Devin-- I'm so sorry, Devin. I'm getting the evil look from my son. I apologize. But we're hoping Devin can come over on Sunday. Thanks. I panicked.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Dad, you fool! [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: How'd that go?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Not well.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Leo's Dad
segments.text: This is my son, Freddy.

segments.speaker: Leo's Dad
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I thought Leo might be upset about it, maybe get sulky. But here he was, cracking up, joking with his dad. It was such a relief to hear him laugh after he'd been so solemn in our interview.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: And I thought, this is all going to be OK. He's going to snap out of it. He's almost there. An afternoon with Devin is going to do the trick. Then, Sunday came.

segments.speaker: Devin
segments.text: OK, now I have three health again.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: I can tell your-- you could tell your wolf to attack.

segments.speaker: Devin
segments.text: OK, I'm going to tell my wolf to attack, then.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Leo taught Devin how to play Dungeons and Dragons.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And the wolf lands on its feet.

segments.speaker: Devin
segments.text: Yay! Go, wolfie! Go, wolfie!

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Devin
segments.text: Go, wolfie! Oh, I am so weird.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: On the drive home, Leo and Devin talk nonstop-- a gentle, rat-a-tat one-upmanship emanating from deep inside a computer game.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: I am a-- I am what else, warlock?

segments.speaker: Devin
segments.text: Warlocks are fun. Can you summon your imp yet?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Yeah, you start with imp.

segments.speaker: Devin
segments.text: Oh, right. I like-- I had a goblin shaman.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: I have a night elf druid. And I can turn into a cat at level eight, which is nice.

segments.speaker: Devin
segments.text: And at level 12, you get a bear.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Devin
segments.text: And then at level--

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: By the time they drop Devin off, they were giggling.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: --yeah, you start with--

segments.speaker: Devin
segments.text: That's funny.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Our cat responds to whatever you call him. [? And he ?] [? said, ?] his name is Pippen, but we can call him Football, and he'll respond.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Devin
segments.text: You call him Football?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Here, Football! Here, Football!

segments.speaker: Leo's Dad
segments.text: Thanks for coming over.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Thanks.

segments.speaker: Devin
segments.text: Thank you for inviting me.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: See you tomorrow.

segments.speaker: Devin
segments.text: See you.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: So a perfect day, right? Leo's parents were relieved, hopeful. But no.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: It's Wednesday. You had your friend over on Sunday. How'd it go?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: It went OK. Yeah, it went OK.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Has it changed anything about being here?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: A little bit. I don't think very much. But a little bit, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: What's changed? What's the little bit?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: That I know someone at school. It helps. Not all that much, but sort of, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: And this is when I realized I'd underestimated the depth of Leo's gloom-- that he greets every morning of every school day with dread, and not because he's being bullied, or anyone's being mean to him.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: I feel sick, because I know that I have the whole day ahead of me, and then I have the next day, and the next day, and the next day, and the next day, and the next day ahead of me.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Does it pass once you get to school?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: No, not really. It usually increases to a climax around lunchtime. And then I-- actually, I've been throwing up recently. And then it just stays at that level of sickness until I get home.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: You're kidding me. You're throwing up at school?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Aw, that's awful. In the bathroom, or where?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Yeah, in the bathroom. Usually at lunch, I feel really bad. And then I go to the bathroom, and I throw up.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Has that happened this week?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Today, it did.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Do you tell your parents like, I don't want to go, I don't want to go? Or do you just-- you know you have to, so you don't say anything?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: No, I throw a screaming fit.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Every morning?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Yeah, pretty much. I didn't today.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: What was different about this morning? How come you didn't today?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: I felt resigned. I mean, I knew that I would have to go anyway, so I gave up.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Here's the curse of being almost 13-- old enough to understand his life will supposedly get better with time, but not old enough to really believe he's going to feel any differently than he does right this minute. Since making friends with Devin, Leo is one step toward being the kid he wants to be-- someone with pals, someone who's comfortable again. But he says right now, he's just worried he's going to be throwing up all year.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Sarah Koenig-- she's the host of Serial. In the years since this story first ran, Leo has made many friends. They've become immersed in the world of theater, and has finally forgiven their parents for the move. Leo did return to New York, though. They graduated from NYU this past spring.
